docs.description: Case name: Pasquantino v. United States Opinion filed: 2005-04-26 Docket No.: 03-725 Citations: • 161 L. Ed. 2d 619 • 125 S. Ct. 1766 • 544 U.S. 349 • 2005 U.S. LEXIS 3701 Case holding summaries: • explaining that absence of such a case prevented Court from "say[ing] with any reasonable certainty whether Congress in 1952 would have considered this prosecution within the revenue rule" • rejecting nonderogation argument when factual differences between common law cases and application of statute were "significant" • "`scheme or artifice to defraud'" • "National [foreign] policy judgments . . . could be undermined if federal courts were to give general effect to wire fraud prosecutions for . . . violating the revenue laws of any country." • "[U]pholding defendants' section 1343 conviction would amount . . . to penal enforcement of Canadian customs and tax laws." • "scheme or artifice to defraud"; "money or property" • holding that § 1341 does not reach schemes to make false statements on a state license application, in part based on reluctance to "approve a sweeping expansion of federal criminal jurisdiction in the absence of a clear statement by Congress" • stating the revenue rule as an exception to the rule that a State enforces foreign judgments, citing, inter alia, pre-1952 cases • declining to interpret the term "`stolen'" in a federal criminal statute according to the common law because the term had "no accepted common-law meaning" • requiring the statute to "`speak directly' to the question addressed by the common law" • holding that a scheme to defraud a foreign nation of tax revenue does not violate the wire fraud statute • holding that the Government of Canada cannot bring a civil RICO suit to recover for a scheme to defraud it of taxes • same with respect to other foreign governments • "The significant fact is the intent and purpose" • stating that the right to collect previously uncollected excise taxes is “„property‟ in [a Government‟s] hands”, and that “[t]his right is an entitlement to collect money . . . , the possession of which is „something of value‟ to the Government. . . .” • holding that a scheme to defraud a foreign nation of tax revenue violates the wire fraud statute • refusing to construe 18 U. S. C. § 1341, the mail fraud statute, to reach corruption in local government, stating: "[W]e read § 1341 as limited in scope to the protection of property rights. If Congress desires to go further, it must speak more clearly than it has." • declining to address "matter . . . not raised or decided below, or presented in the petition for certiorari" • stating that this presumption is applicable "where a common-law principle is well established" • referring to presumption that "legislators take account of the legitimate sovereign interests of other nations when they write American laws" • affirming federal convictions despite the imposition of sentence enhancements, see Brief for Petitioners therein, O. T. 2004, No. 03-1293, etc., p. 7, n. 6 • "When interpreting a statute, we must give words their ordinary or natural meaning" (internal quotation marks omitted) • “To give these same words a differ- ent meaning for each category would be to invent a statute rather than interpret one.” • "[T]he wire fraud statute punishes fraudulent use of domestic wires." • “The right to be paid money has long been thought to be a species of property.” • "the wire fraud statute punishes frauds executed `in interstate or foreign commerce'" (emphasis added) • holding that the wire fraud statute, 18 U.S.C. § 1343, applied to a scheme to smuggle liquor into Canada without paying excise taxes because the statute refers to "communication in interstate or foreign commerce" • suggesting that Cleveland’s construction of the § 1341 (mail fraud) applies equally to § 1343 (wire fraud) • "The mere fact that two federal criminal statutes criminalize similar conduct says little about the scope of either" • holding that evidence of “[p]etitioners’ smuggling operation” satisfied two elements of the federal wire fraud statute • “The right to be paid money has long been thought to be a species of property.” • “The purpose of awarding restitution in this action is not to collect a foreign tax, but to mete out appropriate criminal punishment for that conduct.” • “The 18 purpose of awarding restitution . . . is . . . to mete out appropriate criminal punishment for . . . conduct.” • recognizing a "right to be paid money" as property under mail and wire fraud statutes • “The mere fact that two federal criminal statutes criminalize similar conduct says little about the scope of either.” • holding that "[v]aluable entitlement[]" to be paid taxes is property • holding that evidence of “[p]etitioners’ smuggling operation” satisfied two elements of the federal wire fraud statute • “The right to be paid money has long been thought to be a species of property.” • distinguishing Cleveland and upholding wire fraud conviction for scheme to defraud Canadian government of tax revenue • describing purpose of awarding restitution under MVRA in the case as "to mete out appropriate criminal punishment for that conduct" • holding that evidence of “[p]etitioners’ smuggling operation” satisfied two elements of the federal wire fraud statute • “The right to be paid money has long been thought to be a species of property.” • use of federal wire fraud statute to block interstate communications, in the United States, designed to defraud Canada of tax revenues is not an impermissible extraterritorial application • "[t]he wire fraud statute 9 punishes the scheme, not its success" (internal quotation marks omitted) • "we have construed identical language in the wire 17 and mail fraud statutes in pari materia[, s]ee Neder v. United States, 527 U.S. 1, 20 (1999) 18 ('"scheme or artifice to defraud"')" • noting that whether restitution is mandatory or discretionary does not change government's interest in enforcing orders of restitution • defining "statutory maximum" as "the maximum sentence a judge may impose solely on the basis of the facts reflected in the jury verdict or admitted by the defendant " • “Canada’s right to uncollected excise taxes on the liquor petitioners imported into Canada is ‘property’ in its hands.” • observing that "when con- fronted with two rational readings of a criminal statute, one harsher than the other, we are to choose the harsher only when Congress has spoken in clear and definite language" • “The wire fraud statute punishes the scheme, not its success.” (citations and quotation marks omitted)
